profile.research_note:
Facility specific seeding pass 2026-09-02, batch 36 (Compass Datacenters Red Oak/Ellis County campus): added extensive, well-sourced campus and company history, corroborated a prior sessions unresolved ownership discrepancy toward the Brookfield/Ontario Teachers side without deleting the earlier Redbird Capital mention, explicitly declined to assign a specific address to any of the 11 rows given conflicting aggregator sourcing, two different building-naming conventions in use, and no distinguishing label on any OSM row, an honest gap rather than a guess. research_status remains complete.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Compass Datacenters was founded in 2011 by Chris Crosby, a former senior vice president at Digital Realty, and received a patent in 2014 for a modular data center design. A prior research pass on this row noted an unreconciled ownership discrepancy, the operators own site describing backing from Ontario Teachers Pension Plan and Redbird Capital Partners, versus 2023 trade press describing control by Ontario Teachers Pension Plan together with Brookfield Infrastructure Partners. This sessions fresh Wikipedia check corroborates the trade press side specifically, Brookfield Infrastructure Partners and Ontario Teachers Pension Plan acquired Compass for 5.5 billion dollars in June 2023 and now serve as controlling shareholders, this does not erase the earlier Redbird Capital mention, which is left in place per this projects no-delete policy, but the Brookfield and Ontario Teachers figure is treated as the better corroborated current ownership picture. Compass operates approximately 17 active data centers across the US, Canada, and Israel as of recent reporting. This registry tracks 11 Compass Data Center rows in the Ellis County and Red Oak, Texas area, south of downtown Dallas, all sharing the generic name Compass Data Center with no distinguishing building label in the source data. This is Compasss flagship Texas hyperscale campus, and its scale and naming turn out to be considerably more complex than a simple single-building or even simple-numbered-building site. Per Compass Datacenters own January 2020 groundbreaking announcement, the company purchased 225 acres in Red Oak, Texas for a campus planned to deliver over 350 MW of IT load, with a first six MW building targeted for Q2 2020. Per Dallas Morning News trade press reporting from September 2024 and Data Center Dynamics trade press reporting, the campus grew considerably beyond that first phase, an original 165 acres acquired in 2019 with plans for 16 buildings, expanded to 225 acres in 2020, an additional 375 acres added in April 2023, and most recently a roughly 800 to 830 acre campus footprint approved in May 2026, per that same trade press. At least one 1 million square foot building has already been completed per this reporting, alongside additional phases. Named sub-projects reported in local filings include DFW III-II Buildings 3 and 4, roughly 500,000 square feet combined at an estimated 200 million dollar construction cost targeted for 2025 completion, and DFW III-III Buildings 5 through 7, more than 750,000 square feet combined along Austin Boulevard at street numbers reported as 500, 541, and 581 Austin Boulevard, a roughly 300 million dollar combined construction cost, targeted for completion between 2025 and 2026. Separately, an aggregator directory (Baxtel, tier-5) describes this same overall campus using a different building naming convention, Red Oak I through Red Oak X, giving Red Oak I an address of 300 Houston School Road and Red Oak II through V an address of 481 Austin Boulevard, each building around 251,815 square feet, while a separate aggregator (datacenterHawk) instead assigns 441 N Austin Boulevard specifically to Red Oak I, a direct address conflict between two aggregators over which named building holds which street number. Baxtel separately gives a 155 acre campus total, considerably smaller than the acreage the 2024 to 2026 trade press describes, likely reflecting an earlier, since-superseded campus snapshot rather than a current figure. Given these two different, only partially reconciled building-naming conventions in trade press and aggregator sourcing (Red Oak I-X, and DFW III-II/III-III Building 3 through 7), the direct address conflict between aggregators over Red Oak Is own address, and the fact that none of this registrys 11 OSM-derived rows carry any distinguishing building name or number of their own, this session could not reliably map any specific one of these 11 rows to any specific named building, phase, or street address described above. Asserting a specific address on any individual row here would be a guess this project policy does not permit, so no address is recorded for any of the 11 rows in this campaign, an honest gap given real complexity, not an oversight. The campus also carries real community context, per Data Center Dynamics trade press, local opposition to the most recent 830 acre expansion proposal drew a Change.org petition with more than 2,200 signatures, and Compass responded partly by proposing a 15 million dollar grant to fund a new municipal animal shelter in Red Oak and by establishing a data center technician training partnership with Texas State Technical College, with CEO Chris Crosby stating the company aims to be a 100-year neighbor to Ellis County. No aggregate or building specific megawatt figure confirmed as a current operating capacity was located for this campus in sourcing checked this session, the 350 MW figure from the original 2020 announcement describes a full future build-out target from six years before this research session, not a confirmed current figure, so it is not applied to critical_it_mw for any row. This specific row sits at approximately 32.5441919,-96.802189, part of cluster A (five rows share this campus longitude band) within this registrys 11 tracked rows, a purely geographic grouping observation based on this rows own coordinates, not a claim about which named building or phase it corresponds to.

reading.body:
Compass Red Oak Campus is a multi-phase hyperscale build-out in Ellis County, Texas, south of Dallas, owned by Brookfield Infrastructure Partners and Ontario Teachers Pension Plan following their 2023 acquisition of Compass Datacenters. The operator has not published a current operating capacity for this specific campus. The original 2020 groundbreaking announcement targeted 350 MW of IT load at full build-out across a then-165-acre site; subsequent expansions have grown the approved campus footprint to roughly 800 to 830 acres as of May 2026, with named phases including completed million-square-foot buildings and additional phases under construction or planned through 2026, but no single confirmed current megawatt figure for the operating campus was located in available sources.

This registry maps 11 separate facility rows at this campus location; without distinguishing building names or numbers in the source data, and given conflicting building-naming conventions and address assignments across aggregators and trade press, no individual row can be reliably assigned to a specific named building or street address. The campus sits at coordinates shared with four other mapped rows in a geographic cluster. Texas as a state hosts 133 mapped data center facilities, of which only 18 have published capacity figures totaling 468.41 MW; this campus contributes nothing to that published total and ranks outside the top 18 by confirmed published capacity.

Because the operator has not published current operating capacity, the campus cannot yet be read as a confirmed constraint on AI scaling or supply. The 350 MW full-build-out target from 2020 represents a future state, not confirmed current delivery. If that full target is eventually commissioned, the campus would rank as one of Texas's larger single sites, but that remains a plan rather than an operational fact. The recent 830-acre expansion approval and ongoing construction phases suggest continued build-out activity, but without published megawatt commitments by phase or completion date, the campus's material impact on grid and AI deployment timelines remains unquantified in public data.
